title: Lady Vedehika
hookLine: a mistress well-known for her calm is tested by her maid and loses her temper (MN 21)
last: KAKACUPAMA — A MIND LIKE THE EARTH.

lines: WHAT IS THE CALM RESTING ON?
A STORY HEARD IN A FEW LINES.
cards: When someone stays calm, what is the calm resting on? On day three hundred sixty-three, Vedehika got a few lines: the gentle lady of Savatthi, the maid who slept in, the blow. That telling stopped at the blow.
The Buddha doesn't. In MN 21 he tells the story slowly, gives the maid a mind of her own, and then turns it on his listeners with the question the short version skipped.

teach.b: Start with Kali, because the text does. She isn't lazy. MN 21 calls her clever, diligent and neat in her work.
That's what makes her test clean: there's no real fault to be angry at. Is my mistress truly calm, she wonders, or does the anger just never get a reason? So one morning she gets up late.
Why so late, Kali? No reason, madam. No reason, you wicked girl, and you get up so late?
A frown. The next morning, later, and sharper words.

teach.h: THE THIRD DAY: THE DOOR PIN.
teach.b: The third morning, later still, and Vedehika grabs the pin of the door bolt and strikes her on the head, and it bleeds. Kali goes out and tells the neighbors, and the well-known reputation turns.
Then the Buddha's first point: a monk can seem very gentle, very meek, very peaceful, as long as disagreeable words don't touch him. Then his second, the one the short telling left out.

teach.h: GENTLE ONLY FOR ROBES AND FOOD?
teach.b: He won't call a monk easy to correct if he's easy to correct only so the robes and food keep coming, because when they stop, so does the gentleness.
Only someone who is gentle out of respect for the teaching itself, he says, is truly easy to correct. So the story holds two tests.
Vedehika's calm was resting on nobody pushing. Some calm rests on getting something for it. The Buddha is asking which kind his own monks have.
The story is told to them, not about her, so its edge points inward, at whoever is listening.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of Vedehika to show that patience is known only under provocation, and many practitioners treat everyday irritations as a chance to check their own calm.

o: a queen who gave the Buddha a park
a nun known for answering hard questions
a woman well-known for calm, until her maid tested it

games.q: who did what in the story.

s: Kali was lazy and bad at her work
she did the work well; she got up late on purpose, as a test.
the Buddha says being easy to correct only for robes and food doesn't count
when the robes and food stop, so does the gentleness; he counts only gentleness that comes from respect for the teaching.
the Buddha tells the story to mock Vedehika
it's told to monks, so the edge points at the listeners' own calm.

games.q: you're Kali. your mistress is well-known for her calm, and you wonder if it's real. what does Kali do?
o: asks the neighbors what they think
gets up late on purpose, three days running
games.why: she gets up later each day. by the third, the well-known calm is gone, and so is the reputation.

practice: Bring to mind something mildly irritating, a slow line, a late reply, a noise from next door, and picture it happening once, then a second time, then a third.

Watch where your calm starts to thin: the jaw, the breath, words beginning to form. You're not failing; you're doing what Kali did, but kindly, finding out, and then you can let the picture go and rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Lady Vedehika. Well-known for her calm, until her maid tested it: gentleness is known only when it's tried.

carryVoice: Your line: calm, tested. Real gentleness doesn't depend on nobody pushing. Day four hundred eighteen, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (the story of Vedehika and Kali)
